motion: Is the Christian God worthy of worship?

bridges.description: Connect the Christian conception of God as maximally great and morally perfect to the conclusion that this God is maximally worthy of worship.
Connect Christian commitments about canonical unity, Jesus, and love to a morally coherent reading of difficult biblical depictions.
Connect genre, historical context, and whole-text reading to resistance against isolated face-value indictments of God.
Connect longstanding interpretive diversity and creed-level restraint to the claim that Christianity need not endorse genocidal or violent readings.
Connect literary depth and a clear broad redemptive message to an explanation of why detailed disagreement need not show failed divine communication.
Connect the depicted divine violence, threats, and harms to the conclusion that the Christian God is not morally worthy of worship.
Connect Rauser's perfection and Jesus principles to a challenge that the framework assumes the favorable conclusion it is used to protect.
Connect dependence on disagreeing experts and traditions to the charge that an all-wise caring God communicated ineptly.
Connect the standpoint of victims of conquest and rape imagery to rejection of later theological reframing as an adequate moral answer.
Connect the preservation of violent human speech without explicit condemnation to a challenge about inspiration and moral authority.

sections.title: Starting points and reading the Bible
sections.rationale: The opening dispute establishes each side's method: Christian contextual and genre-sensitive reading versus face-value initial reading, independent moral judgment, and concern about disagreeing experts.

sections.title: Inspiration, human voices, and the Psalms
sections.rationale: Psalm 137 and Psalm 14 test whether canonical inclusion preserves human lament within a larger teaching or transmits morally damaging claims without adequate correction.

sections.title: Violence, conquest, and divine agency
sections.rationale: Rape imagery and conquest narratives are the central concrete evidence bearing on whether the depicted Christian God is loving and worship-worthy.

sections.title: Clarity, diversity, and conditional frameworks
sections.rationale: The parties directly dispute whether Christian interpretive commitments are warranted, whether disagreement signals failed communication, and whether ambiguity can have literary value.

sections.title: Worship, religious harm, and fallibility
sections.rationale: The religion-as-cancer exchange, the final moral denunciation, and the closings connect the textual dispute to worship, human consequences, and shared acknowledgment of fallibility.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Christians understand God as a maximally great being and therefore as maximally worthy of worship.
moves.warrant: Rauser invokes the Anselmian maximal-greatness conception while qualifying that not every Christian uses that terminology.
moves.inference: If the Christian God is the maximally great being Christians confess, worship-worthiness follows as part of that conception.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Rauser's stated core Christian conception and ends when he completes the explicit worship-worthiness inference, before turning to the book.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Christians believe God is a maximally great being
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator directly handed the discussion to Rauser, and the first-person opening continues without interruption.
moves.audioVerificationReason: One of the six supplementary automated checks confirms this opening definition and distinction; no direct listening is claimed.
moves.importanceRationale: This is Rauser's direct motion-level ground for an affirmative answer.

burdenContact.rationale: It explicitly links the Christian conception of divine perfection to worship-worthiness.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Barker's book builds a one-sided negative case by collecting passages selected to support its prior conclusion.
moves.warrant: Rauser notes that almost all chapters address negative attributes, cites Barker's invitation to scan emphasized words, and says the presentation largely places verses one after another without their contexts.
moves.inference: That selective presentation is insufficient by itself to establish the biblical depiction of God without fuller contextual engagement.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span resumes after the chapter-count interjection and retains Rauser's complete one-sided-case and missing-context reasoning through the completed sentence that the method uses the text as a pretext for ideological ends.
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser owns the selected post-interjection argument continuously; the earlier chapter-count exchange is outside this boundary.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The automated opening check confirms the contextual-reading critique; no additional audio verification is represented.
moves.importanceRationale: It challenges the reliability of the con side's recurring textual evidence.

burdenContact.rationale: The move argues that context and literary handling are necessary before a passage can bear the con side's moral inference.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Beginning with a text's face value does not commit Barker to literalism, because metaphor and literary reasons can justify moving beyond it.
moves.warrant: Barker explicitly cites Jesus as lamb and door as obvious metaphors and describes the Bible as a collection of writings with literary value.
moves.inference: Rauser's fundamentalist label does not by itself defeat Barker's stated method of starting with ordinary meaning and then considering reasons for figurative interpretation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span starts with Barker's direct answer to the fundamentalism charge and includes his complete lamb-and-door examples, ending when he transitions to his fictional-character premise.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: we do have to start with the face value, even if you then later conclude that it's metaphorical
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator explicitly gives Barker the floor, and Barker's first-person reply is continuous.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The supplementary Barker check confirms the face-value starting point and explicit acceptance of metaphor.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves the con side's actual interpretive burden and answers a central opening objection.

burdenContact.rationale: It establishes Barker's claimed nonliteralist method before he challenges the Christian framework layered onto the text.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the characterization of Barker's method as fundamentalist by stating when face value may properly yield to metaphor or literary context.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: A God who requires expert mediation while experts and traditions disagree has communicated an essential message poorly.
moves.warrant: Barker contrasts the importance attributed to scripture with the absence of an accompanying expert and catalogs conflicting denominational and scholarly authorities.
moves.inference: Persistent expert disagreement undermines the expectation that an all-wise, caring communicator delivered an accessible message.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This extended but indivisible opening argument moves from the importance of the alleged divine message, through the need for experts, to disagreement among candidate authorities and Barker's resulting moral reading; the full chain is needed to preserve the distinction between needing expertise and experts disagreeing.
moves.attributionRationale: Barker speaks continuously after his interpretive-method reply and before Rauser's question.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The supplementary Barker check confirms the need-for-experts challenge and disagreement among experts.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the main con bridge from interpretive disagreement to alleged divine ineptitude.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the full communication-failure argument from expert dependence and disagreement.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: There is no universal default face-value setting for reading ancient texts; genre and historical-cultural distance must guide interpretation.
moves.warrant: Rauser notes that a modern reader encounters translated texts from alien contexts and may need scholarship while still grasping the broad scriptural message.
moves.inference: The need for occasional expert help does not make the text wholly opaque or vindicate a wooden initial reading.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The narrowed span begins when Rauser resumes after Barker's interjection and contains his genre, historical-distance, and occasional-scholarship answer through the completed commentary example.
moves.attributionRationale: This boundary excludes Barker's objection and the moderator's turn-management remarks; Rauser supplies the selected genre and historical-distance reasoning.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct listening was performed; ownership follows the named handoff and first-person continuity.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the pro side's direct answer to Barker's methodological and communication challenge.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains why contextual and genre-sensitive reading is required without claiming perfect detailed clarity.

responseComponents.description: Disputes the claimed need to begin from a face-value default and substitutes genre-sensitive reading.
Answers the expert-dependence objection by distinguishing broad accessibility from immediate mastery of every ancient passage.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Psalm 137 preserves anguished human lament rather than God commanding or endorsing the dashing of infants.
moves.warrant: Rauser identifies the speaker as an exiled psalmist and compares the rage to a bereaved mother's curse against the person who killed her family.
moves.inference: Charitable attention to trauma can explain why the canon preserves the expression without treating the rage as its final moral teaching.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins with Rauser's Psalm 137 example, identifies the human speaker, and completes the bereaved-mother analogy and preservation rationale before Barker responds.
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser introduces the Psalm example and maintains first-person explanatory continuity throughout.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source notes specifically confirm the function and limits of the bereaved-mother analogy.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the pro side's principal contextual answer to one of Barker's strongest moral texts.

burdenContact.rationale: It applies contextual and canonical reading to distinguish preserving lament from divine endorsement.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Acknowledging that Psalm 137 voices a human author raises the unresolved question of why such morally ugly words belong in inspired scripture.
moves.warrant: Barker accepts that an exiled human psalmist expresses anger but asks where the line is drawn if flawed human speech is included as God's word.
moves.inference: Identifying the immediate human speaker does not by itself answer the objection from canonical inclusion and moral authority.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Barker's two-part answer, preserves his acknowledgment of human authorship and anger, and ends after his explicit line-drawing challenge; this complete sequence is necessary to avoid misrepresenting his objection as confusion about who spoke.
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser has directly asked Barker to explain his claim, and Barker's response is continuous in this span.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source notes confirm Barker acknowledges human authorship; no direct listening is claimed.
moves.importanceRationale: It states the con side's central inspiration objection in the Psalm exchange.

burdenContact.rationale: It shifts the burden from immediate speaker identity to why inspired canon preserves the violent wish.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the human-lament explanation but argues that it leaves the inspiration, inclusion, and moral-authority question unresolved.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Canonical participation in human anger does not validate that anger as the moral endpoint; Jesus' command to love enemies supplies the Christian endpoint.
moves.warrant: Rauser distinguishes understanding rage from vindicating it and reads the Psalm within a canon culminating in Jesus' teaching.
moves.inference: The Psalm can accompany readers through painful emotion while the canon directs them beyond bitterness and revenge.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This compact reply contains the precise distinction between identifying with emotions and validating them, followed by the Jesus-based canonical endpoint.
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser answers Barker's expanded objection in a continuous, clearly owned turn.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source restrictions expressly preserve this validate-versus-final-teaching distinction.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the pro side's direct moral answer to canonical inclusion of the violent wish.

burdenContact.rationale: It uses the Jesus and love principles to identify the canon's claimed final moral direction.

responseComponents.description: Answers why the lament may remain in scripture by distinguishing truthful representation of rage from its canonical moral endpoint.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The text leaves the violent wish standing without explicit condemnation, making Rauser's Christian endpoint an imposed sermon rather than the passage's clear teaching.
moves.warrant: Barker insists no one should celebrate killing infants and says an explicit denunciation should appear somewhere rather than relying on a scholarly framework.
moves.inference: If condemnation must be supplied from outside the passage, the canon communicates its moral lesson inadequately.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span captures Barker's complete response: the charge of importing Jesus, the moral objection to the wish, and the absence-of-condemnation communication challenge.
moves.attributionRationale: Barker's first-person reply follows Rauser's canonical conclusion without a speaker change.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source notes identify the absence of explicit condemnation as Barker's preserved challenge.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly contests whether Rauser's contextual reading resolves the moral communication problem.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that inclusion without explicit correction leaves a morally dangerous canonical message.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the claimed canonical endpoint as an overlay and demands explicit textual condemnation of the violent sentiment.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: A Christian reads difficult texts through four linked commitments: divine perfection, canonical unity, Jesus as interpretive center, and love of God and neighbor.
moves.warrant: Rauser separately defines each principle and connects scripture's use to teaching, correction, righteousness, and love.
moves.inference: Within Christianity, apparently immoral passages should be interpreted consistently with the character revealed in Jesus and the canon's loving purpose.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins where Rauser enumerates the four principles and ends after he completes the love principle; retaining all four is necessary because the contract distinguishes them and their combined inference.
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser explicitly lays out his own interpretive framework in a continuous response.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source notes identify and distinguish all four principles; no direct listening is claimed.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the central pro framework governing nearly every later textual reply.

burdenContact.rationale: It explicitly supplies the Christian inference rules that connect difficult texts to a loving conception of God.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: The perfection and Jesus principles protect the desired conclusion by assuming in advance that God cannot be cruel or mistaken.
moves.warrant: Barker notes that the framework rules out divine imperfection before the disputed texts are evaluated and overlays a later Christian lens on the Hebrew scriptures.
moves.inference: Internal coherence under Christian commitments does not independently establish that the favorable interpretation is true.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Barker's direct response to the four principles and completes his circularity, Jesus-overlay, and independent moral-judgment objections before he returns to rape imagery.
moves.attributionRationale: Barker takes the floor after Rauser finishes the framework and speaks continuously.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source notes explicitly require preserving Barker's challenge to the conditional Christian commitments.
moves.importanceRationale: It contests the evidential force of the pro side's central interpretive framework.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the framework secures internal consistency only by building the favorable divine character into its premises.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the framework as assumption-driven and denies that a non-Christian is obligated to adopt it.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Even if lifting skirts is metaphorical, the passage attributes wartime sexual violation to God's own punitive agency.
moves.warrant: Barker describes the invasion context and emphasizes the reported first-person divine statement, 'I myself will lift up your skirts.'
moves.inference: Calling the wording metaphorical does not remove the moral problem of God claiming agency in rape imagery and punishment.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins where Barker returns to the part he says Rauser ignored, preserves his express concession that the wording may be metaphorical, and completes the divine-agency moral challenge.
moves.attributionRationale: Barker explicitly signals the point Rauser allegedly ignored and speaks continuously through the completed challenge.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source restrictions specifically require preserving metaphorical qualification and divine agency.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a central concrete challenge to the Christian God's moral worthiness.

burdenContact.rationale: It links a specific depiction of divine agency in sexualized violence directly to unworthiness.

responseComponents.description: Concedes possible figurative language but argues that contextual and metaphorical classification does not remove the divine-agency charge.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Core Christianity does not commit Christians to one interpretation of every violent biblical passage.
moves.warrant: Rauser distinguishes the creed's claims about the triune God and salvation from disputed theories of atonement and readings of Isaiah, Exodus, and Canaan.
moves.inference: A morally troubling reading of a particular passage cannot simply be equated with what Christianity centrally teaches about God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The passage begins with Rauser's direct response, identifies his assumptions, then gives the complete creed-versus-particular-text distinction through the Canaanite example.
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser takes the floor immediately after Barker's challenge and maintains a continuous first-person reply.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source notes expressly require preserving the creed-versus-scripture distinction.
moves.importanceRationale: It limits the pro side's burden regarding disputed violent passages without claiming they are irrelevant.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that creed-level Christian identity permits multiple approaches to morally difficult texts.

responseComponents.description: Limits the theological inference from Barker's preferred reading by separating disputed passage interpretation from creedal Christianity.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Barker uses cancer as a metaphor for religion's harmful effects on minds and actions rather than as a literal description.
moves.warrant: When challenged, Barker explicitly identifies the word as metaphorical and explains the comparison in terms of infection of thought and conduct.
moves.inference: The metaphor is intended as criticism of religious effects, though its breadth remains open to Rauser's objection.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span captures Barker's initial defense of the metaphor and his own stated harmful-effects meaning, while excluding the longer back-and-forth over particular examples.
moves.attributionRationale: Barker supplies the metaphor explanation in this short exchange; Rauser's brief challenge is context and is not used as Barker's support.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source notes preserve the metaphor with its qualifications; the mild overlap does not require a mixed event boundary.
moves.importanceRationale: It bears on the claimed real-world moral stakes while requiring careful qualification.

burdenContact.rationale: It connects Barker's textual critique to claimed harmful religious effects without making demeanor an assessment category.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Unqualified description of religion as cancer can otherize and dehumanize people and is itself a form of harmful rhetoric.
moves.warrant: Rauser emphasizes the breadth of the category religion and argues that sweeping disease language can facilitate exclusion and violence.
moves.inference: A critic of biblical violence should also scrutinize the harmful potential of his own generalizing rhetoric.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This narrow turn contains Rauser's complete rhetoric objection, from the breadth of religion through the otherizing consequence and self-application challenge.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator asks Rauser for a quick comment, and Rauser owns the entire selected response.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct listening was performed; named handoff and clear turn structure establish ownership.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a substantive reply about the moral effects of Barker's retained main-discussion rhetoric.

burdenContact.rationale: It applies Rauser's demand for definition and qualification to Barker's broad rhetoric about religion.

responseComponents.description: Argues that Barker's metaphor remains overly broad and harmful despite its figurative meaning.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Barker distinguishes attacking religion and its claimed harms from attacking Christians as people.
moves.warrant: He says most Christians are good, denies attacking Rauser personally, praises Rauser's life and family, and reiterates that cancer is a metaphor for a problem.
moves.inference: The broad metaphor should be read as criticism of beliefs and institutions, not as denial of believers' humanity.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This later reply contains Barker's explicit people-versus-religion distinction, praise of Christians and Rauser, and metaphor qualification, ending before the next Psalm example.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator asks Barker whether he should qualify the statement; Barker owns the continuous answer selected here.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No direct listening was performed; ownership follows the explicit moderator handoff and coherent first-person response.
moves.importanceRationale: It materially qualifies the retained religion-as-cancer claim and answers Rauser's harm objection.

burdenContact.rationale: It narrows Barker's real-world harm claim to religion and religious ideas rather than religious persons.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Psalm 14's language is used to depict people who deny God as corrupt and incapable of good, harming and dehumanizing atheists.
moves.warrant: Barker quotes the fool and no-good language, identifies himself as a nonbeliever, and asks whether Rauser thinks he has ever done good.
moves.inference: A canon that brands nonbelievers this way undermines its claimed love and moral authority.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The narrow span contains Barker's complete personal application of Psalm 14 and his test question, before Rauser begins his contextual reply.
moves.attributionRationale: Barker introduces Psalm 14 in response to the rhetoric discussion and directly addresses Rauser.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source notes specifically preserve the Psalm 14 dispute; no direct listening was performed.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies a distinct harm-based challenge to the moral effects of scriptural interpretation.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that canonically retained language can harm a class of readers even apart from physical-violence narratives.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Reading the whole Psalm makes its subject universal human fallenness and need for restoration, not a targeted assertion that atheists alone never do good.
moves.warrant: Rauser closes the exchange by insisting that the reader continue beyond the first clause and states the Psalm's universal subject.
moves.inference: Barker's self-application does not establish that Psalm 14 uniquely dehumanizes atheists.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This narrow concluding passage is Rauser's clean own-speaker summary of the whole-Psalm reading and avoids the earlier interleaved dispute over practical atheism and hyperbole.

moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers a distinct allegation that the text condemns atheists as such.

burdenContact.rationale: It applies whole-Psalm context to argue for a universal-fallenness reading rather than an atheist-specific indictment.

responseComponents.description: Answers Barker's atheist-specific application by summarizing the whole Psalm as addressing universal human fallenness and restoration.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Rauser's Jesus-centered reading is conditional on Christianity being true and would lose its warrant if Jesus did not rise and Christianity were false.
moves.warrant: In answer to the moderator's counterfactual, Rauser says one would no longer assume divine superintendence or be justified in Christological readings of Isaiah and Psalm 137.
moves.inference: Acknowledging conditional premises is not question-begging by itself; competing readers can expose their assumptions and critically compare results.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span starts with Rauser's answer to the moderator's counterfactual and ends after his explicit appeal for all readers to recognize their starting assumptions.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator directly addresses Rauser, whose answer remains continuous through the selected span.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The supplementary resurrection-context check confirms this conditional answer and ownership.
moves.importanceRationale: It clarifies the logical status of the pro framework and directly answers the circularity charge.

burdenContact.rationale: It limits the framework to a conditional Christian inference rather than presenting internal coherence as independent proof.

responseComponents.description: Concedes the framework's dependence on Christianity while denying that openly held starting assumptions are uniquely illegitimate.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: A Christian can naturally use a Christian lens, but sincere Christians still reach sharply different conclusions, so the lens does not resolve the communication problem.
moves.warrant: Barker grants the internal point and immediately appeals to historical Christian disagreement and conflict before reaffirming neutrality as his preferred starting place.
moves.inference: Conditional reasonableness inside Christianity does not show that the text reliably communicates a determinate moral message.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Barker's answer after the moderator's terminal question fragment, preserving his internal concession and disagreement challenge through the resurrection qualification.
moves.attributionRationale: Bertuzzi supplies the preceding question, recorded separately as context; Barker owns the selected concession and disagreement reasoning.

burdenContact.rationale: It grants internal Christian reasoning while arguing that ongoing Christian disagreement still bears on clarity.

moves.speaker: Dan Barker
moves.claim: Later Christian redemptive framing does not make conquest morally loving from the standpoint of its victims.
moves.warrant: Barker imagines a Canaanite woman facing an Israelite sword and asks whether explaining Jesus and a later moral arc would alter the immediate killing.
moves.inference: A framework that cannot justify the harm to those subjected to it fails to establish the depicted God's worship-worthiness.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The selected sequence starts with Barker's announced Old Testament example, develops the victim-centered thought experiment, and ends with his explicit rejection of both atheist and Christian big-picture justifications.
moves.attributionRationale: Barker continues after answering the moderator's internal-reasonableness question and owns the first-person thought experiment.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source notes specifically preserve this victim-centered Canaanite challenge.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the con side's strongest direct moral test of conquest interpretations.

burdenContact.rationale: The move evaluates the conquest narrative from the perspective of the harmed people rather than later doctrinal outcomes.

responseComponents.description: Argues that interpretive latitude and later Christian framing still owe an account of the immediate harm to depicted victims.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Christian interpretation includes several materially different approaches to conquest, including accommodation, hyperbolic warfare, spiritual readings, and denial that God commanded the violence.
moves.warrant: Rauser surveys Calvin and Merrill, Wright, Copan and Flannagan, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, and Boyd, explaining the distinct function of each approach.
moves.inference: Barker cannot treat the most literal genocidal reading as the only Christian account against which worship-worthiness must be judged.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The unusually long span is required because Rauser's warrant is the source-specific diversity of several nonmergeable interpretive approaches and their different treatments of command, history, hyperbole, spiritual meaning, and Jesus; it ends at his explicit synthesis that Christians share moral indignation without creedal commitment to one reading.
moves.attributionRationale: Rauser is invited to offer Christian approaches and delivers one uninterrupted extended survey before Barker answers.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source notes require preserving the surveyed diversity without treating every listed view as Rauser's own.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the pro side's main answer to conquest as motion-level evidence.

responseComponents.description: Answers that Barker's victim-centered objection bears on some readings but does not exhaust the Christian interpretive options.

moves.claim: The recurrence of commands involving whole groups, women, children, and animals resists dismissal as an isolated or merely figurative difficulty.
